title: Why Orwell Still Matters: Reason 3621
author: Greg O'Keefe
summary: Greg O'Keefe uses his experience teaching 1984 to a resistant student as a case study in how postmodern relativism, absorbed into school culture as atmosphere rather than doctrine, has produced students who mistake institutional permission to validate their own interpretations for genuine epistemic independence. The student's conviction that his reading is as valid as the teacher's is not self-generated critical thinking — it is a permission structure handed down by an institution that rewards validated feelings over genuine intellectual challenge. O'Keefe connects this to Orwell's own radical empiricism: the conviction that seeing clearly is a moral act, and that the Ministry of Truth's deepest crime was not lying but destroying the capacity to care about the difference between truth and falsehood. The tragic irony is that students trained to resist external standards of truth are reading 1984 — the book most precisely engineered to expose exactly that process — and coming away more committed to relativism.
points: The postmodern turn in literary pedagogy was never really philosophy — it was a permission structure that protected teachers, rubrics, and students from discomfort while insulating students from the rigour of being wrong.

O'Keefe's example of the school owner who told students mid-class that Animal Farm was 'just one man's opinion' illustrates how relativism functions as a tool of institutional power rather than liberation from it.

A classroom where all interpretations are equal is a classroom where no one fails, no one is uncomfortable, and no difficult conversation about evidence and warrant ever quite lands — the teacher and the institution are protected more than the student.

Orwell was a radical empiricist who believed seeing clearly was a moral act; his consistent through-line from Homage to Catalonia to 1984 was the refusal to let the institution pre-answer the question.

The central diagnostic question O'Keefe poses: if a student reads 1984 and emerges more committed to the idea that no external standard of truth exists, did the book fail — or did the institution succeed?
quotes: My student didn't arrive at his interpretive confidence on his own. It was given to him by a school culture that has absorbed, in diluted and well-intentioned form, the postmodern turn in literary theory. The message, transmitted not as doctrine but as atmosphere, is something like: your response to a text is inherently valid. Meaning lives in the reader. There are no wrong answers, only under-explored ones.

It doesn't free the student from authority. It insulates him from the discomfort of being wrong, dresses that insulation in the language of epistemology, and hands it to him as a gift from the institution. He now carries institutional permission to dismiss any reading that ranks above his own.

Postmodern relativism in schools was never really philosophy. It was a permission structure. And like all permission structures, it serves the institution at least as much as the student. A classroom where all interpretations are equal is a classroom where no one fails, no one is uncomfortable, and no difficult conversation about evidence and warrant ever quite lands.

Orwell was not a relativist. He was a radical empiricist who believed that seeing clearly was a moral act, not merely an intellectual preference. The through-line is the same: the refusal to let the institution pre-answer the question. The Ministry of Truth's deepest crime wasn't lying. It was destroying the capacity to care about the difference.

That capacity is precisely what a certain strain of well-meaning pedagogy has been quietly eroding. Not through malice. Through comfort. Through the slow institutional preference for students who feel validated over students who have been genuinely challenged.
If he reads 1984 and comes away more committed to the idea that no external standard of truth exists, did the book fail? Or did the institution succeed?
